cim_eredeti: Delphi Study Identifies Human Factors Priorities for Clinical Artificial Intelligence Integration
szoveg_eredeti:
Delphi Study Identifies Human Factors Priorities for Clinical Artificial Intelligence Integration

Integrating computational tools into everyday hospital environments introduces complex operational challenges that require careful coordination among clinical workflows, medical staff, and healthcare technologies, according to a modified Delphi consensus study published in Human Factors in Healthcare. Researchers led by Katharina Wenderott, Jim Krups, Matthias Weigl, and Abigail R. Wooldridge investigated how human factors and ergonomics experts evaluate the real-world deployment of artificial intelligence systems in clinical settings. By consulting international specialists across a two-stage consensus process, the study sought to identify core considerations for safely weaving automated algorithms into healthcare practice. The research team emphasized that artificial intelligence in healthcare cannot be understood as an isolated piece of software, but rather as an evolving collection of computational methods—including decision tree learning, neural networks, and clustering algorithms—that interact dynamically within intricate sociotechnical work environments composed of organizational rules, medical devices, and frontline personnel.

The study was motivated by persistent implementation hurdles and the recognition that predictive tools developed under controlled laboratory parameters frequently encounter unforeseen operational barriers when deployed in live clinical settings. Grounding their inquiry in human factors and ergonomics, the investigators examined interactions across micro-, meso-, and macro-ergonomic levels. The International Ergonomics Association defines the discipline as the scientific pursuit concerned with understanding interactions among humans and other system elements, applying theory, principles, and methods to optimize human well-being and overall system performance. In modern clinical environments, this perspective addresses critical safety phenomena, such as automation bias, clinical handovers, interprofessional communication, and situational awareness. Although computational algorithms hold promise for predicting surgical complications, reducing hospital-acquired infections, and preventing adverse drug events, their introduction can destabilize established workflows if cognitive workload, usability, and systemic fit are neglected during development and operational rollout.

To capture expert consensus systematically, the authors conducted a modified Delphi inquiry comprising two consecutive phases, adhering to the standardized DELPHISTAR reporting framework for health and social sciences. The study received ethical approvals from the Ethics Committee of the Medical Faculty of the University of Bonn and the Institutional Review Board at the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign, with pre-registration completed in the German Clinical Trials Register under registration number DRKS00034254. In the first phase, the investigators conducted qualitative, semi-structured video interviews with ten subject-matter experts in human factors and ergonomics who held professorial appointments and extensive healthcare backgrounds. These specialists, consisting of five women and five men with an average age of 50.6 years and an average professional experience of 20.2 years, represented institutions in the United States, Australia, and Israel. Seven of the ten interviewees were actively conducting healthcare-related artificial intelligence research, focusing on predictive models, clinical decision support systems, observational machine learning data, and technology-enabled operating rooms.

The interview transcripts, generated verbatim using automated transcription tools and manually corrected, underwent structured qualitative content analysis using MAXQDA software. Two researchers independently coded the interview data across three central categories: recommendations for artificial intelligence implementation, positive impacts on healthcare, and negative impacts on healthcare. From an initial extraction of 161 recommendation-related segments and 272 impact-related segments, the investigators synthesized 26 distinct implementation recommendations and 17 patient safety items. Recommendations mentioned by at least two interviewees were converted into Likert-scale items for the subsequent evaluation round. The statements were categorized across simplified operational lifecycle stages: design and development, implementation processes, monitoring, evaluation, education, and regulatory policy.

In the second Delphi round, the study team administered an online questionnaire to evaluate participant agreement on a seven-point Likert scale ranging from 1, representing strong disagreement, to 7, representing strong agreement. The survey recruited 39 participants, with two respondents excluded due to unvarying response patterns or incomplete submissions, yielding an analytical sample of 37 professionals. This sample consisted of 27 human factors specialists and 10 healthcare professionals, with an overall average work experience of 15.38 years and a median of 15 years. Participants represented a geographically diverse cohort across ten countries, with the United States comprising 17 respondents, followed by Germany with four, the United Kingdom with four, Ireland with three, Australia with two, China with two, and single participants from Austria, Brazil, Canada, and Israel. The survey also evaluated participants’ baseline artificial intelligence literacy using a shortened 11-item Scale for the Assessment of Non-Experts’ AI Literacy, alongside the Shinners’ Artificial Intelligence Perception tool.

Consensus among panel members was defined a priori using a rigorous threshold requiring at least 80 percent of participants to rate an item with a 6 or 7 on the agreement scale. Out of the 26 surveyed implementation recommendations, 22 achieved this strict consensus criterion. The highest consensus rates emerged around early system design, extensive pre-deployment testing, and clinical verification. Specifically, 97.30 percent of respondents agreed that organizations must identify appropriate tasks for automation before initiating technical design, analyze clinical workflows to evaluate how tools affect staff, and extensively test software performance prior to clinical integration. Similarly, 97.30 percent agreed on establishing incident reporting mechanisms for events involving automated systems and evaluating implementation success in actual clinical practice. Furthermore, 94.59 percent agreed that human-centered principles must govern the entire lifecycle from development to evaluation, developers must understand clinician workflows, and deployed tools must undergo regular operational monitoring to ensure continued proper functioning.

User-centered design and stakeholder involvement were strongly affirmed throughout all stages of technology adoption. Approximately 89.19 percent of panel participants agreed that tools should feature user-friendly interfaces that make critical clinical information readily identifiable, provide structured user training during clinical rollout, and incorporate artificial intelligence education into medical and healthcare curricula. In addition, 91.89 percent emphasized that unique organizational contexts must be accounted for during deployment, and that regulatory institutions must publish dedicated policies to govern safe clinical use. Regarding organizational rollout strategy, 86.49 percent supported conducting small-scale pilot deployments, sharing institutional implementation experiences across healthcare organizations, and encouraging researchers and publishers to disseminate diverse evaluation studies, including practice-based implementation reports and negative results.
